article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education: nine categories of educator-used generative AI tools
description: A taxonomy arranging generative AI tools used in educational contexts into nine categories: General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, Audio and Music Generation Tools, Video Generation Tools, Presentation Generation Tools, Research and Study Tools, AI Tutoring and Chatbots, Custom Education Tools, and Other Miscellaneous Tools. It continues the authors' earlier Web 2.0 and free web-based learning technology typologies, and each tool receives a brief description and link so educators can judge fit for their teaching and learning contexts.
requirements: Tools included must have been reported by two or more educators and be publicly available with a free version
constraints: Not an exhaustive list; represents a snapshot of educator-reported usage in 2025-2026
Some tools offer functionality across multiple categories
target_learners: educators across early childhood, elementary, high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: informed selection of generative AI tools aligned with pedagogical goals and values
examples: ChatGPT appears in the General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, and Presentation Generation Tools categories, reflecting educators' use of this tool for multiple purposes
key_sources: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData

citation: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328
title: Typical versus maximal performance distinction as an explanation for absent real-world consequences of cognitive decline
description: This explanatory account holds that everyday outcomes reflect typical functioning whereas cognitive tests assess maximal functioning, so age-related deficits appear only when demands approach maximal levels. The review states: "what we do in daily life reflects our typical level of functioning, whereas cognitive tests attempt to assess our maximal level of functioning". Because people seldom need to function at their maximum, declines may go undetected in daily-life criteria. The review presents this as the first of four candidate explanations for the lab-life discrepancy.
requirements: Outcome criteria must reflect typical rather than maximal performance for the discrepancy to arise
constraints: The account does not deny real declines; it holds they are not detected because people seldom function at the level where deficits would appear
target_learning_goals: explaining why laboratory-measured cognitive declines do not necessarily impair everyday occupational and daily functioning
examples: The review contrasts the age distribution of top-scoring reasoning performers, which peaks before age 30, with the age distribution of Fortune 500 CEOs, which peaks near 60
key_sources: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328
